Let me think about the proof strategy. This is the classic "free theorem" for System F: any closed term of type ∀X. X → X, applied to a value v of type U, can evaluate to v.

But here, we have nondeterminism, so the theorem only requires *some* reduction path ending in v.

Approach: Logical relation.

Standard approach: define a logical relation `R_T : tm -> tm -> Prop` (binary, "type-indexed") relating terms at type T. Actually the problem says "construct an appropriate binary, type-indexed logical relation; define the interpretations of type-variable and term-variable contexts; prove the typing-rule obligations and a fundamental theorem".

Since types may have free type variables (fvar) and bound variables (bvar), we need a semantic interpretation of types. Since there's a ty_context (list of atoms) and types are locally nameless with free variables as atoms... interesting: variables like Ty_FVar X are atoms, and Ty_All is represented with bound variable 0 via open_ty.

The classic approach in the locally nameless style: interpret types relative to an environment mapping type variables (atoms) to relations, and for bound variables, we handle them via "open" with the atom of an extended environment.

A common way: define the logical relation as a Fixpoint on ty, parameterized by:
- a type environment (list of atoms, Delta) — actually the ty_context says which free vars are in scope
- an interpretation for free variables: each atom X gets a binary relation on terms (or a pair of a type and a relation)
- the interpretation for bound variables: use a list of relations for de Bruijn indices.

Since Ty_BVar indices refer to bound type variables, which are introduced by Ty_All. When interpreting under a ty_context Delta, index 0 refers to the most recent binder. We can maintain a list of relations indexed by de Bruijn index, and for free variables look them up in an atom-indexed environment.

Actually because of the locally nameless convention, when we do open_ty T (Ty_FVar X) for a fresh X, the free variable X is used. So the key question remains: how is [[∀X.T]]ρ defined to make this work with arbitrary R and arbitrary U?

In Reynolds' original formulation, the interpretation of ∀X.T is given by intersection over all *relations* R on the semantic domain, and the type application t[U] is interpreted by applying the semantic function to the relation [[U]] — the relation interpreting the type U. So the instantiation uses [[U]], not an arbitrary R! The free theorem then says: for t : ∀X.T, the semantic value ⟦t⟧ maps any relation R to an element of ⟦T⟧[X:=R]; and the *syntactic* type application t[U] denotes ⟦t⟧(⟦U⟧), using R = ⟦U⟧.

So the free theorem as usually stated (Wadler): given t : ∀X.T, types A, B, relation R ⊆ A×B, if... you get a relation between t[A] and t[B]. But here's the subtlety: in Wadler's free theorem, the relation at X is arbitrary, and the types A and B are *the types at which t is instantiated*, with R a relation between A-values and B-values. The semantic interpretation of the *type application* t[A] uses ⟦t⟧ applied to ⟦A⟧, but the abstraction theorem says ⟦t⟧ is parametric: it maps *any* relation R to a related pair, regardless of what R is. In the semantic model, t's semantic value is a function from relations to values — because t : ∀X.T is interpreted in the *parametric* model where the universal type is an intersection over ALL relations (not just those arising from types). That's the key: the interpretation of ∀X.T in the logical relation is an intersection over all relations, so ⟦t⟧(R) ∈ ⟦T⟧[X:=R] for ANY R. And separately, the *syntactic* application t[A] has semantic meaning ⟦t⟧(⟦A⟧). So to connect t[A] with an arbitrary R, we need the "type application is interpreted by the relation of the type" — but the logical relation is a *syntactic* relation between terms, not a semantic model.

In the syntactic logical relation setting, the standard trick is: define the relation on terms at type ∀X.T as:

```
Fixpoint ty_subst_all (σ : atom -> ty) (T : ty) : ty :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar i => Ty_BVar i
  | Ty_FVar X => σ X
  | Ty_Arrow T1 T2 => Ty_Arrow (ty_subst_all σ T1) (ty_subst_all σ T2)
  | Ty_All T1 => Ty_All (ty_subst_all σ T1)
  end.
```

Note: free type vars only (no de Bruijn handling needed; bound vars are de Bruijn). Similarly `tm_ty_subst_all σ t` replacing all free type vars in annotations:
```
Fixpoint tm_ty_subst_all σ t :=
  match t with
  | tm_abs T t1 => tm_abs (ty_subst_all σ T) (tm_ty_subst_all σ t1)
  | tm_tapp t1 T => tm_tapp (tm_ty_subst_all σ t1) (ty_subst_all σ T)
  ...
  end.
```
And term substitution `tm_subst_all (γ : atom -> tm) t`.

Definitions:
```
Definition rel := tm -> tm -> Prop.

(* Environment for free type variables: triple of (left type, right type, relation) *)
Definition ty_env := atom -> (ty * ty * rel).

Definition bound_env := list (ty * ty * rel).

Fixpoint V (binds : bound_env) (rho : ty_env) (T : ty) : tm -> tm -> Prop := ...
```
But V and E are mutually recursive (E uses V, V's arrow clause uses E at subterms). Since E uses V and V uses E at structurally smaller types, mutual recursion on the type works:

```
Fixpoint E (binds) (rho) (T) (s1 s2 : tm) : Prop :=
  locally_closed_tm s1 /\ locally_closed_tm s2 /\
  exists v1 v2, s1 -->* v1 /\ s2 -->* v2 /\ V binds rho T v1 v2
with V (binds) (rho) (T) (v1 v2 : tm) : Prop :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar i => nth i binds (default triple) relation v1 v2
  | Ty_FVar X => let '(_,_,R) := rho X in R v1 v2
  | Ty_Arrow A B => forall u1 u2, E binds rho A u1 u2 -> E binds rho B (tm_app v1 u1) (tm_app v2 u2)
  | Ty_All A => forall A1 A2 R, locally_closed_ty A1 -> locally_closed_ty A2 -> E (A1,A2,R)::binds rho A (tm_tapp v1 A1) (tm_tapp v2 A2)
  end.
```

Let's think about what the type substitution lemma actually needs. The relation [[T]] is defined by recursion on T; at Ty_FVar X it applies rho(X)'s relation. The lemma [[open_ty T U]]ρ = [[T]](binds := (Uσ1,Uσ2, ?)::binds) needs the relation component for the bound variable to be *the interpretation of U*, in the sense that at a base position, the substituted U's occurrences (which are subterms of the type U, not a variable) get interpreted recursively. That's why the environment maps variables to relations in a way that's compositional: for the lemma to hold, the environment's relation for the bound variable must be exactly the interpretation of U, i.e., [[U]](ρ, binds) — which for arrow types is the arrow relation, etc. So the bound env triple can't just carry a `rel`; it must be interpreted compositionally. Alright, let me also think about the type substitution lemma's statement and proof more concretely, since it's central.

```
Fixpoint V (binds : list rel) (rho : atom -> rel) (T : ty) : tm -> tm -> Prop :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar i => match nth_error binds i with Some R => R | None => fun _ _ => True end
  | Ty_FVar X => rho X
  | Ty_Arrow A B => fun v1 v2 => forall u1 u2, E binds rho A u1 u2 -> E binds rho B (tm_app v1 u1) (tm_app v2 u2)
  | Ty_All A => fun v1 v2 => forall A1 A2 R, locally_closed_ty A1 -> locally_closed_ty A2 -> E (R :: binds) rho A (tm_tapp v1 A1) (tm_tapp v2 A2)
  end
with E (binds : list rel) (rho : atom -> rel) (T : ty) (s1 s2 : tm) : Prop :=
  locally_closed_tm s1 /\ locally_closed_tm s2 /\ exists v1 v2, s1 -->* v1 /\ s2 -->* v2 /\ V binds rho T v1 v2.
```

Hmm, for the BVar case using nth_error with a default: the type substitution lemma's BVar case needs the index to be in range. Let me define:
```
Definition nth_rel (i : nat) (binds : list rel) : rel :=
  match nth_error binds i with Some R => R | None => fun _ _ => True end.
```

The type substitution lemma with insert_at:
```
Fixpoint insert_at (k : nat) (R : rel) (l : list rel) : list rel :=
  match k with
  | 0 => R :: l
  | S k' => match l with [] => [R] | x :: l' => x :: insert_at k' R l' end
  end.
```

So the lemma:
```
Lemma V_open_ty_rec : forall k T U binds rho,

And fty_tm/ty should be defined as "free type atoms in annotations", ftv_tm as free term variables.

Standard binary logical relation for System F with explicit type application:

Define interpretations of types as relations on terms, in an environment where:

But the crucial question is how to define the ∀ case so that the TApp typing rule is provable AND the free theorem "∀X.T at arbitrary R" gives us statements about t[U].

The standard parametricity theorem for System F says: If t : ∀X.T (closed), then for all types A, B, and relations R between "values of A" and "values of B", and related a R b, then t A a and t B b are related at T[X:=R]. Here the relation R is on terms, but the *terms* a and b live at types A and B; the relation R need not be type-respecting in the syntactic setting. This is the standard "free theorem" from Wadler's paper: for t : ∀X. X→X, for all A,B, R ⊆ A×B: if (a,b) ∈ R then (t A a, t B b) ∈ R.

In Wadler's setup, R is a relation on the *semantic* domains of A and B. In the syntactic setting with untyped terms, R can be an arbitrary relation on closed terms, and "a : A" and "b : B" are just typing facts used to justify... hmm, actually they're needed for the typing of the application and for the fundamental theorem to apply. But the logical relation itself, at base type variable X, uses R regardless of A and B.

The trick for our theorem: we pick A = B = U, a = b = v, R = {(x,y) | x -->* v ∧ y -->* v}. The free theorem gives (t U v, t U v) ∈ R — i.e., t U v -->* v.

```coq
(* ===== Utilities: free variables ===== *)

Fixpoint fta_ty (T : ty) : list atom :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar _ => []
  | Ty_FVar X => [X]
  | Ty_Arrow A B => fta_ty A ++ fta_ty B
  | Ty_All A => fta_ty A
  end.

Fixpoint fta_tm (t : tm) : list atom :=
  match t with
  | tm_bvar _ => []
  | tm_fvar _ => []
  | tm_abs T b => fta_ty T ++ fta_tm b
  | tm_app a b => fta_tm a ++ fta_tm b
  | tm_tabs b => fta_tm b
  | tm_tapp b T => fta_tm b ++ fta_ty T
  | tm_choice a b => fta_tm a ++ fta_tm b
  end.

Fixpoint ftv_tm (t : tm) : list atom :=
  match t with
  | tm_bvar _ => []
  | tm_fvar x => [x]
  | tm_abs _ b => ftv_tm b
  | tm_app a b => ftv_tm a ++ ftv_tm b
  | tm_tabs b => ftv_tm b
  | tm_tapp b _ => ftv_tm b
  | tm_choice a b => ftv_tm a ++ ftv_tm b
  end.

Fixpoint fbv_ty (T : ty) (i : nat) : Prop :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar j => i = j
  | Ty_FVar _ => False
  | Ty_Arrow A B => fbv_ty A i \/ fbv_ty B i
  | Ty_All A => fbv_ty A (S i)
  end.
```

Substitution envs:

```coq
Definition tyenv := atom -> ty.
Definition tmenv := atom -> tm.

Fixpoint subst_ty_env (σ : tyenv) (T : ty) : ty :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar i => Ty_BVar i
  | Ty_FVar X => σ X
  | Ty_Arrow A B => Ty_Arrow (subst_ty_env σ A) (subst_ty_env σ B)
  | Ty_All A => Ty_All (subst_ty_env σ A)
  end.

Fixpoint subst_tm_ty_env (σ : tyenv) (t : tm) : tm :=
  match t with
  | tm_bvar i => tm_bvar i
  | tm_fvar x => tm_fvar x
  | tm_abs T b => tm_abs (subst_ty_env σ T) (subst_tm_ty_env σ b)
  | tm_app a b => tm_app (subst_tm_ty_env σ a) (subst_tm_ty_env σ b)
  | tm_tabs b => tm_tabs (subst_tm_ty_env σ b)
  | tm_tapp b T => tm_tapp (subst_tm_ty_env σ b) (subst_ty_env σ T)
  | tm_choice a b => tm_choice (subst_tm_ty_env σ a) (subst_tm_ty_env σ b)
  end.

Fixpoint subst_tm_env (γ : tmenv) (t : tm) : tm :=
  match t with
  | tm_bvar i => tm_bvar i
  | tm_fvar x => γ x
  | tm_abs T b => tm_abs T (subst_tm_env γ b)
  | tm_app a b => tm_app (subst_tm_env γ a) (subst_tm_env γ b)
  | tm_tabs b => tm_tabs (subst_tm_env γ b)
  | tm_tapp b T => tm_tapp (subst_tm_env γ b) T
  | tm_choice a b => tm_choice (subst_tm_env γ a) (subst_tm_env γ b)
  end.
```

Let me define:
```
Definition rel := tm -> tm -> Prop.
Definition stack := nat -> rel.
Definition empty_stack : stack := fun _ => fun _ _ => False.
Definition push_stack (R : rel) (st : stack) : stack := fun i => match i with 0 => R | S j => st j end.
Definition set_stack (st : stack) (m : nat) (R : rel) : stack := fun i => if Nat.eqb i m then R else st i.
```

Fixpoint V_ty (st : stack) (rho : atom -> rel) (T : ty) : rel :=
match T with
| Ty_BVar i => st i
| Ty_FVar X => rho X
| Ty_Arrow A B => fun v1 v2 => forall u1 u2, value u1 -> value u2 -> V_ty st rho A u1 u2 ->
    (exists w1 w2, value w1 /\ value w2 /\ tm_app v1 u1 -->* w1 /\ tm_app v2 u2 -->* w2 /\ V_ty st rho B w1 w2)
| Ty_All A => fun v1 v2 => forall R U1 U2, lc_ty_at 0 U1 -> lc_ty_at 0 U2 ->
    (exists w1 w2, value w1 /\ value w2 /\ tm_tapp v1 U1 -->* w1 /\ tm_tapp v2 U2 -->* w2 /\ V_ty (push_stack R st) rho A w1 w2)
end.

Definition E_ty (st : stack) (rho : atom -> rel) (T : ty) (t1 t2 : tm) : Prop :=
  exists w1 w2, value w1 /\ value w2 /\ t1 -->* w1 /\ t2 -->* w2 /\ V_ty st rho T w1 w2.

Note E_ty's definition refers to V_ty ✓ defined before.
